title: Just arrived in the UK: how do I register with a GP? Can I do it without proof of address or an NHS number?
summary: How to register with a GP in England: ways to apply, what documents are needed, what to do if you are refused, plus temporary registration and interpreting services.
content:
# Just arrived in the UK: how do I register with a GP? Can I do it without proof of address or an NHS number?

Last updated: 2026-11-27

> This guide covers **England**. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland do things a little differently, and we will cover them separately.

In the UK, a GP is usually your first stop for everyday healthcare. A GP is a general practitioner (a family doctor), and a GP practice (often called a GP surgery) is the local family doctors' clinic in your community. For things like a cold or fever, repeat prescriptions for long-term medicines, or a referral to a hospital specialist, you normally go through your GP first. So once you are living in England, registering with a GP practice is something you will need to do sooner or later.

When they first arrive, many people get stuck because they feel they "don't have the right documents": they have only just rented a home and no Council Tax or utility bills have arrived yet; they do not have an NHS number; their passport or visa documents may be somewhere else while an application is processed. In fact, none of this stops you registering with a GP. Below we go through it one step at a time, in the order you are likely to come across things.

## Should I register as soon as I arrive?

There is no need to wait. If you only start looking for a practice and filling in forms once you are ill, it is much more stressful. Once you have more or less settled where you are living, you can get started.

If you have come to study and live near your university for most of the year, register with a GP near your university. Many universities have their own health centre, and registering there is usually the most convenient option. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-student-local-gp)

Children under 16 are usually registered by a parent or guardian. The NHS website notes that the practice may ask to see proof of the child's identity or address, and may ask for confirmation that the person registering them is their parent or guardian. This does not change the general rule that registration does not depend on providing proof of identity, proof of address, immigration documents or an NHS number. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-children-under-16-registration)

## How to find a practice and apply

Enter your postcode on the NHS website to find GP practices near you. Most people register with a practice near where they live, because each practice covers its own area; some practices are also willing to accept people who live a bit further away. Check the practice's website or give them a call to find out.

There are a few ways to apply:

- fill in a form online on the NHS website, which takes about 15 minutes;
- go to the practice reception and ask for a paper form. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-first-gp-registration-routes)

## Can I register without proof of address?

Yes. You do not need proof of address to register with a GP in England.

Having no bills yet because you have just moved is completely normal. NHS England's guidance for practices is clear: not being able to show proof of identity or proof of address is not a reasonable ground for refusing registration, and it cannot be used as a reason to refuse you an appointment. If you cannot produce any proof at all, but you tell the practice that you live within its area, the practice should accept your registration. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-registration-without-address-proof)

So on the form, just write the address where you actually live now, whether that is a place you have just rented or somewhere you are staying temporarily.

## Do I need a passport, BRP or eVisa?

No. Registering with a GP does not require you to prove your identity or your immigration status. Practice staff are not responsible for checking visas: the British Medical Association (BMA) says in its guidance for practices that staff should not be treated as immigration officers. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-registration-without-identity-immigration-proof)

According to NHS England's guidance, students, people on work visas, people seeking asylum, people with no fixed address and overseas visitors can all register with a GP practice, whether or not they are lawfully in the UK. Seeing a GP (a consultation) is itself free of charge. Seeing a hospital specialist or staying in hospital is covered by a separate set of rules, which is a different matter from GP registration and is not covered here. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-gp-eligibility-and-free-consultations)

There is one more situation: your passport or other documents may currently be with the Home Office (the UK government department that handles visas and immigration) for a visa application, so you do not have them with you. NHS England's guidance specifically lists this as an example of "genuinely being unable to produce documents", and the practice should still deal with your registration. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-documents-held-by-home-office)

## So why is reception asking for my documents?

This does happen. The rules allow a practice to have its own policy of asking all new patients to show documents. The main reason is to match you accurately on the national patient system, so that your previous medical records can be transferred to you and future referrals are not mixed up with someone else.

However, there are some limits:

- if a practice asks for documents, it must treat all new patients the same way, not just certain people;
- it should not routinely ask for photo ID;
- if you genuinely cannot provide documents, the practice must have another way of dealing with this and cannot refuse to register you because of it. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-practice-document-policy-limits)

If you have it, show the document a practice asks for. If you do not have it, explain your situation, for example: “I’ve just arrived and don’t have proof of address yet.” The NHS registration page explains which documents you do not need. NHS England’s patient information also lists resources in different languages.

## What if I don't have an NHS number?

An NHS number is a 10-digit number. Everyone has their own, and it is used to find you and your health records on NHS systems.

You do not need an NHS number before you register with a GP. If you have never used NHS services in England before, you will be given one when you first register with a GP, and it will be in the letter you receive once your registration is complete. If you forget it later, you can find it in the NHS App or phone your practice to ask. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-registration-without-nhs-number)

## What if a practice refuses to register me?

A practice can refuse to register you, but it must have a reasonable ground. Common ones are:

- the practice is not taking on new patients at the moment;
- you live outside the area the practice covers.

Race, gender, age, religion, appearance, disability or health condition cannot be used as reasons for refusal, and, as mentioned above, neither can being unable to show documents. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-reasonable-refusal-grounds)

If you are refused, the practice must tell you the reason in writing within 14 days. Once you have the reason, you can: [See the official source](#guide-evidence-written-refusal-within-fourteen-days)

- apply to another practice nearby;
- contact your local integrated care board (ICB, the organisation that arranges local NHS services);
- ask Citizens Advice or your local Healthwatch for help.

While you are not yet registered, if you have a problem that needs to be dealt with straight away, GP practices have a contractual duty to provide emergency or immediately necessary treatment free of charge for up to 14 days. This applies even to a practice that has refused to register you. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-unregistered-immediately-necessary-care)

## Only staying a few months: temporary registration

If you are staying somewhere for more than 24 hours but less than 3 months, you can apply for temporary registration. For example, a family member may come to stay in England for a month or two, or a student may leave their university town during the holidays and spend some time in another city.

Temporary registration lasts for up to 3 months. When it ends, you can apply again or apply to register as a permanent patient. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-temporary-registration-duration)

## My English isn't very good. Can I ask for an interpreter?

Yes. When you book an appointment, tell the practice that you need an interpreter and which language you need. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-request-interpreter)

The relevant NHS England guidance recommends offering a qualified interpreter and discourages relying on family members or friends to interpret. Children under 16 must not act as interpreters; the only exception is in exceptional circumstances where immediate and necessary treatment is required. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-free-interpreter-and-safeguarding)

## After you have registered

Practices usually complete your registration within about 5 days of receiving your details, but it may take longer. Once it is done, you will receive a letter with your NHS number on it. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-registration-processing-time)

To contact your practice, you can go in person, phone, or get in touch online through the practice website or the NHS App between 8am and 6:30pm, Monday to Friday. For contact that is not clinically urgent, the practice should respond appropriately by the end of the next working day at the latest, telling you what will happen next. This does not mean you will necessarily get an appointment or have the matter resolved within that time. If the practice decides that something is clinically urgent, it should take appropriate action on the same day; this does not necessarily mean a face-to-face appointment that day. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-gp-contact-hours-and-response)

If you move later and want to change practice, just register with the new practice. You do not need to tell your old practice first; the system will deal with it automatically. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-change-practice-without-notifying-old)

## What to do in practice

1. Once you have somewhere to live (temporary is fine), start looking for a practice.
2. Enter your postcode on the NHS website to find nearby GP practices and check whether they are taking on new patients.
3. Apply online or fill in a form at reception.
4. Bring documents if you have them, and apply anyway if you do not. Not having proof of address or an NHS number does not matter. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-registration-without-address-proof)
5. If English is difficult for you, say that you need an interpreter when you book. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-request-interpreter)
6. If you are refused, ask for the reason in writing and try another practice. If that still does not solve the problem, contact your local ICB, Citizens Advice or Healthwatch. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-written-refusal-within-fourteen-days)
7. Look out for the letter from the practice and make a note of your NHS number.

evidence.statement: Students who live near their place of study for most of the year should register with a GP near their university.

supports.locator: 1. Register with a local GP
supports.note: Supports choosing a GP near the university based on where the student mainly lives during the year; a university health centre is usually convenient, but students do not have to choose it.

evidence.statement: A first registration can be made by applying online on the NHS website or by filling in a paper form at the practice.

supports.locator: Register or change GP surgery online; Other ways to register with a GP surgery
supports.note: Supports applying online or on paper; the NHS App is not treated as a route for first registration. Whether online registration is available depends on whether the practice offers it.

evidence.statement: Being unable to provide proof of address is not a reasonable ground for refusal; if a person says they live within the practice area, the practice should accept their registration.

supports.note: Having no proof of identity or address documents is not in itself a reasonable ground for refusal; keeps the conditions that the person lives within the practice area and that there is no other reasonable ground for refusal, and keeps the strength of "should accept".

supports.locator: What you need to register with a GP surgery
supports.note: Confirms that proof of address is not needed; a temporary address can be used, and people with no fixed address can also register.

evidence.statement: Registering with a GP does not require proof of identity or proof of immigration status; staff are not responsible for acting as immigration officers.

supports.note: There is no regulatory requirement to provide proof of identity or immigration status; a practice policy of asking for documents is allowed if it is non-discriminatory and has reasonable exceptions.

supports.locator: Registering without proof of identity or address
supports.note: Supports the point that staff should not act as immigration officers; it is not a promise that no medical data will ever be shared.

evidence.statement: In England, immigration status does not affect eligibility to register with a GP or to receive free NHS GP consultations; hospital services have separate rules.

supports.note: Supports that the groups listed are eligible to apply for GP registration without first meeting the conditions for free hospital treatment; it does not guarantee that any particular practice will accept them unconditionally.

supports.locator: Tourists and overseas visitors; Patients with no immigration status
supports.note: Supports that NHS GP medical services are not charged for on the basis of immigration status; this does not extend to hospital services or private letters.

supports.locator: GP services; Hospital treatment
supports.note: GP registration and eligibility for hospital charges are separate matters; free GP care should not be taken to mean that all NHS services are free.

evidence.statement: Documents being held by the Home Office for an application can be a reasonable exception where a person genuinely cannot show documents.

supports.note: The guidance explicitly lists the situation where documents have been handed to the Home Office; supports treating this as a reasonable exception, without removing other lawful grounds for refusal.

evidence.statement: A practice's document policy should be consistent and non-discriminatory, should not routinely require photo ID, and should deal with exceptions where a person genuinely cannot provide documents.

supports.note: The policy allows practices to ask for documents, but it must be applied fairly; photo ID is "should not routinely", and being unable to provide documents cannot in itself be a reasonable ground for refusal.

evidence.statement: You do not need an NHS number before registering with a GP; one can be allocated at first registration and provided in the registration letter.

supports.locator: What you need to register with a GP surgery
supports.note: The number helps match records, but it is not a precondition for registration.

supports.locator: How to find your NHS number; How to get an NHS number
supports.note: Supports getting a number at first registration and finding it in the registration letter or the NHS App; the number is not treated as the same thing as eligibility for free treatment.

evidence.statement: Refusing registration requires a reasonable ground, such as the list being closed or the person living outside the practice area; registration cannot be refused because of a protected characteristic or a lack of documents.

supports.note: Supports reasonable and limited grounds for refusal and the ban on discrimination; having previously been removed from a list is not presented as a general ground for refusal.

evidence.statement: A practice that refuses registration must explain the reason in writing within 14 days of the decision.

supports.locator: Version 7, §4.11.3
supports.note: This is a "must" requirement with a 14-day limit, not just a recommendation.

supports.locator: Who can register with a GP surgery — If a surgery does not accept your registration
supports.note: Also explains that people can contact the ICB, Citizens Advice or Healthwatch for help.

evidence.statement: When a person is not registered or has been refused registration, GPs have a contractual duty to provide emergency or immediately necessary treatment free of charge for up to 14 days.

supports.locator: Duty to provide emergency treatment
supports.note: The contractual duty applies to eligible people in the practice area, including people who have been refused registration or are temporarily registered; immediately necessary treatment depends on clinical judgement and does not mean any routine treatment.
Supports clinically necessary emergency or immediately necessary treatment and the related 14-day protection; it does not guarantee any particular appointment.

evidence.statement: People staying for more than 24 hours but less than 3 months can apply for temporary registration; it lasts up to 3 months, after which they can apply again or apply for permanent registration.

supports.note: People who meet the length-of-stay condition should be offered the option of temporary registration; this is a route to apply, not automatic approval by any particular practice.

supports.locator: Registering with a GP surgery as a temporary patient
supports.note: Supports the maximum of 3 months and that, when it ends, people can apply again for temporary or permanent registration; the page also acknowledges that an application may be refused.

evidence.statement: To change GP, you only need to register with the new practice; you do not need to tell your old practice first.

supports.locator: Register or change GP surgery online — changing surgery information
supports.note: The old practice is informed automatically once the new registration is made; patients are not required to tell their old practice first.
